The last table is the one to watch over a season: a clue you lean on often that sits near 50%
isn't earning its place. The two guesser lines are the honest comparison. Guessing "pass" on
every snap is right about 60% of the time in today's NFL, so a 60% log hasn't shown any reading
at all. How much better can you do, and where does the improvement come from? Here is what
simple rules would have scored over the 2025 season:

```{python}
#| label: fig-bar-to-beat
#| fig-cap: "The bar to beat. Accuracy of simple run-or-pass guessers on every 2025 regular-season run and dropback (32,813 snaps). Each rule was learned from the 2024 season (for every combination of its inputs it guesses whichever was more common in 2024) and then scored on 2025, the way your own guesses are made before the fact. The situation on the scorebug gets you from 60% to about 68%; one glance at the quarterback's alignment adds about seven points more. Source: nflverse play-by-play and FTN charting."
p24 = plays_with_alignment(2024)


def prep(d):
    d = d.copy()
    d["dist"] = pd.cut(d.ydstogo, [0, 3, 6, 99], labels=["1-3", "4-6", "7+"])
    d["late"] = (d.half_seconds_remaining <= 120).astype(int)
    d["score"] = pd.cut(d.score_differential, [-99, -9, -1, 0, 8, 99], labels=["d9+", "d1-8", "tie", "u1-8", "u9+"])
    d["q4"] = (d.qtr >= 4).astype(int)
    return d


train, test = prep(p24), prep(p25)


def accuracy(keys):
    if not keys:
        return float((test["pass"] == 1).mean())
    rule = train.groupby(keys, observed=True)["pass"].mean().rename("p_pass").reset_index()
    m = test.merge(rule, on=keys, how="left")
    guess = (m.p_pass.fillna(train["pass"].mean()) >= 0.5).astype(int)
    return float((guess == m["pass"]).mean())


LADDER = [("Always guess pass", []),
          ("Down & distance only (like your 01-02 tally)", ["down", "dist"]),
          ("+ score, quarter and clock", ["down", "dist", "score", "late", "q4"]),
          ("+ the quarterback's alignment", ["down", "dist", "score", "late", "q4", "qb_location"])]
vals = [accuracy(k) for _, k in LADDER]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.5))
ys = np.arange(len(LADDER))[::-1]
cols = [style.MUTED, style.OFFENSE, style.OFFENSE, style.THIRD]
ax.barh(ys, vals, color=cols, height=0.58, zorder=2)
for y, v in zip(ys, vals):
    ax.text(v + 0.006, y, f"{v:.0%}", va="center", ha="left", fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
ax.axvline(0.5, color=style.INK_2, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=3)
ax.text(0.505, ys[0] + 0.45, "coin flip", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2, ha="left", va="center")
ax.set_yticks(ys, [n for n, _ in LADDER], fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlim(0.4, 0.82)
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
ax.set_xlabel("share of 2025 snaps called correctly (run vs pass)")
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
plt.show()
```

Three lessons hide in that chart.[^ladder] First, as the scorebug section warned, **down and
distance alone barely beat "always pass."** It is decisive on the downs where it's lopsided,
but first-and-10, the most common situation by far, is close to a coin flip (about 50% pass in
2025), so a rule built only on down and distance guesses "pass" there and gets half of them
wrong. Second, across a whole game the **score and the clock add more than the down does**:
late in a half, and when a team is behind, the run-pass mix swings hard. Third, **one glance at
the formation is worth almost as much as everything on the scorebug combined.** The coaches know
this too; it is why the best offenses work so hard to run and pass from the same looks.

So the targets for your own log are clear. If you are under 60%, you're doing worse than a
guesser who never looks up. Around 65–68%, you're reading the scorebug well. Above 70%, the
formation and the tells are working for you. Don't be surprised if your first log lands in the
low 60s; that is what the scorebug alone is worth before you have practised reading it.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper: why the confidence column?"}
"Right or wrong" throws away information. A 55% call that misses and a 90% call that misses are
very different mistakes, and a good reader knows the difference before the snap. That's why the
log has a confidence column even though we score only hits and misses for now: it costs one
number per snap. [Film Study: All-22, Charting a Game, and Scoring Yourself](../15-capstone/15-02-film-study-and-charting.qmd)
scores the season's log the way forecasters are scored, by whether your 70% calls come true
about 70% of the time. Until then, the only thing to log beyond run or pass is nothing: one
prediction per snap, made *before* the snap, is plenty. As the course goes on, chapters add
columns (which side the run goes, which receiver gets the ball, whether the safeties rotate,
whether the defense blitzes), and by the end your log is a full pre-snap read.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday: prediction log, game 1"}
For one half of one game, on every offensive snap of one team:

- **During the pause**, read the scorebug in order (down and distance, field position, score,
  clock, timeouts), glance at the quarterback's and back's alignment (and any motion, the
  movement you counted in [The Pre-Snap Phase](01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd)), and say "run" or "pass"
  out loud *before the snap*, with a rough confidence (55%, 70%, 85%).
- **Write the line** during the replays: at least down, to-go, call, confidence, and the clue
  word (sit, align, stance, safety).
- **After the play**, record what happened, using the rules above (sacks and scrambles are
  passes; skip kneel-downs, spikes and plays wiped out by penalties).
- **On the replays**, pick one thing (@tbl-one-thing) and check one clue you used: was the hand
  really heavy? Where did the safety go?
- **At halftime**, score it. Compare it with your down-and-distance tally from
  [Downs, Distance, and Field Position](01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd), with the two
  guessers, and with the bar to beat above. Keep the sheet; the course will come back to it.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: third-and-1"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-short
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-1 at the opponent's 38, second quarter, tied 7–7. The offense comes out under center with two tight ends and a fullback (U and Y are the tight ends, F the fullback, R the tailback, seven yards deep). On the close-up before the snap, the linemen's down hands are heavy. The defense has crowded the line: nine defenders within five yards of the ball, a cornerback on the lone wide receiver and one safety deep (on defense, S is the Sam linebacker and SS the strong safety)."
off = offense("i_form_22")
off = [p_.moved(label="R") if p_.key == "RB" else p_ for p_ in off]
dfn = defense("4-3_over", "single_high", off)
adj = {"MIKE": dict(d=3.5), "WILL": dict(d=3.5), "SAM": dict(d=3.0), "SS": dict(d=5.0, w=7.6),
       "WDE": dict(w=-5.7), "LCB": dict(d=4.0, w=-7.4), "RCB": dict(d=6.0), "FS": dict(d=11.0)}
dfn = [p_.moved(**adj[p_.key]) if p_.key in adj else p_ for p_ in dfn]
q1 = Play(off, dfn, los=72, to_go=1)
q1.highlight("RB", color=style.THIRD)
fld = q1.draw(lateral=(-18.5, 18.5), window=(-9.5, 13.5), title=False)
# a bracket behind the five linemen: the label is about the whole line, not one gap
(bx0, by0), (bx1, by1) = [tuple(map(float, fld.xy(*q1.to_abs(-1.75, w_)))) for w_ in (-3.6, 3.6)]
(tx0, ty0), (tx1, ty1) = [tuple(map(float, fld.xy(*q1.to_abs(-1.35, w_)))) for w_ in (-3.6, 3.6)]
fld.ax.plot([tx0, bx0, bx1, tx1], [ty0, by0, by1, ty1], color=style.INK_2, lw=1.1, zorder=9)
pointer(fld, q1, "heavy hands\nall along the line", (-4.2, -10.5), (-1.75, -1.2))
pointer(fld, q1, "tailback at\n7 yards", (-7.4, 6.2), (-7.0, 0.8))
plt.show()
```

**Run or pass? How confident are you, and what is the one thing to watch at the snap?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Run, about 85%.** Third-and-1 is the most run-heavy situation in football: in 2025, teams ran
on about three in four third-and-1s, and from under center they ran on about 84%.[^short] A good
share of those runs never reach the tailback: about three in ten of the under-center snaps on
third-and-1 were quarterback sneaks (the push-from-behind version, the tush push, is in
[Red Zone, Goal Line, and Short Yardage](../10-situational-football/10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd)).
The defense agrees with you, which is why nine defenders are crowded near the line.

**Why not higher, when every clue points the same way?** Because the clues aren't independent.
Two tight ends, a fullback, under center and a deep tailback travel together: that is simply
what a short-yardage formation looks like, and the 84% already counts all of them. Adding them
up again would be counting the same evidence three times. The heavy hands add even less here:
on short yardage every lineman is heavy on every snap, run or play-action, so in this picture
the stance tells you nothing new. Stance earns its keep on ordinary downs.

**Your one thing:** the line of scrimmage (the short-yardage row of @tbl-one-thing), from the
end-zone angle if you get it on the replay. Whose linemen move forward first and farther? On
short yardage that yard of push decides the play before the ball carrier arrives.

**And the other 15%?** This is exactly the picture play-action is built for. With nine
defenders charging the line and one safety deep, a fake handoff and a pass to a tight end
sneaking out behind the linebackers is the classic counterpunch. A good log line here is
"R, 85%, align." If it turns out to be a play fake, that is not a bad prediction; it is the 15%.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: the safety who walks into the picture"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-safety
#| fig-cap: "First-and-10 near midfield, shotgun with the back beside the quarterback. The grey is what your TV shot leaves out. The defense first showed two deep safeties at 13 yards (the outlined ghosts, both off your screen). With about eight seconds on the play clock, the safety on the offense's right walks down to eight yards, just outside the right tackle, and into the top of your picture; the other slides over toward the deep middle, still off screen (dashed arrows)."
q2 = base_play(to_go=10, los=58.0)
moves = {"SS": ((13.0, 9.5), (8.0, 5.0)), "FS": ((13.0, -9.5), (14.0, -1.5))}
for k_, (_, (d_, w_)) in moves.items():
    q2.players[k_] = q2.players[k_].moved(d=d_, w=w_)      # where they are now
q2.highlight("SS", color=style.THIRD)
fld = q2.draw(lateral=(-20, 20), window=(-8.5, 19.5), title=False)
shade_outside(fld, q2, tv_footprint(1.5, 0.0, *TV_WIDE), alpha=0.55)
for k_, ((gd, gw), (nd, nw)) in moves.items():
    (gx, gy), (nx, ny) = [tuple(map(float, fld.xy(*q2.to_abs(d_, w_)))) for d_, w_ in ((gd, gw), (nd, nw))]
    fld.ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((gx, gy), 4, radius=0.75 * 1.5, orientation=np.pi / 4, fc=style.SURFACE,
                                    ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), zorder=14))
    fld.ax.text(gx, gy, k_, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.5, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, zorder=14)
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((gx, gy), (nx, ny), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=11, color=style.DEFENSE,
                                     lw=1.5, ls=(0, (3, 2)), shrinkA=9, shrinkB=12, zorder=14))
pointer(fld, q2, "showed two deep,\nthen walks down late", (17.0, 14.5), (13.8, 10.2))
label(fld, q2, "▲ top edge of\nyour TV picture", (8.2, -7.6), fs=6.8, color=style.INK_2)
plt.show()
```

**On your TV, what tells you this happened, and how should it change your run-or-pass lean?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**What you'd see:** not the walk itself, which starts off screen, but its arrival. A defender
appears at the top edge of the picture where nobody stood a moment ago and settles a few yards
off the ball. Other on-screen hints: count the defenders near the line, which goes from six to
seven; linebackers may shift over to make room; the quarterback may point, shout or change the
call ([The Pre-Snap Phase](01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd)); and the analyst, who has a wider
monitor, often says it ("they're rotating a safety down"). The other safety sliding to the
middle you won't see live; that is the skycam replay's job.

**What it means:** the defense went from two-high to one-high, and now has seven defenders in
the box against six blockers (five linemen and the back). That is the picture from 01-05's
second drill, and the logic is the same: against seven in the box a run has a free defender,
so many quarterbacks check out of a run into a pass, and run-pass options throw into the space
behind the safety who came down.

**Your lean:** nudge it *toward* pass, but only a little. First-and-10 from the shotgun was
already a passing look (72% pass in 2025).[^gun110] Two things keep you from going much higher.
With eight seconds left the quarterback may not have time to check, and the walk-down may be a
bluff: some safeties race back to the deep middle at the snap, the disguise game of
[Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd).
Something like "P, 75%, safety" is a good line, and if you never saw the safety arrive, the clue
is "align" and the lean stays where the shotgun put it.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: which clue wins?"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-clues
#| fig-cap: "Second-and-6 at the offense's own 40, third quarter, ahead 14–10. Shotgun with trips to the right, the tight end attached to the line (Y, H and Z), and the back offset to the quarterback's left. On the left, the lone receiver (X) has a reduced split, about eight yards outside the center instead of out near the numbers, and his cornerback has followed him in. The linemen are in two-point stances. Two safeties deep."
off = offense("gun_trips")
off = [p_.moved(w=-7.8) if p_.key == "X" else p_ for p_ in off]
dfn = defense("nickel", "two_high", off)
dfn = [p_.moved(d=6.5, w=-8.8) if p_.key == "LCB" else p_ for p_ in dfn]   # slight outside leverage
q3 = Play(off, dfn, los=50, to_go=6)
q3.highlight("X", "RB", color=style.THIRD)
fld = q3.draw(lateral=(-20, 23), window=(-8.5, 16.5), title=False)
pointer(fld, q3, "X: reduced split", (-5.2, -14.0), (-0.7, -8.6))
pointer(fld, q3, "back offset\nto QB's left", (-6.6, -6.6), (-5.0, -2.3))
plt.show()
```

**Five clues: second-and-6, shotgun, the back's offset, X's reduced split, two deep safeties.
Run or pass, and what does each clue tell you?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Pass, about 70–75%.** Weigh the clues in order of strength, broad ones first:

1. **Second-and-6** on its own is a coin flip: about 52% pass in 2025 for second-and-medium.
2. **Shotgun** moves it a long way. In 2025, teams passed on 76% of their shotgun snaps on
   second-and-5 to -7. That is your call. (The two-point stances agree, but standing linemen are
   common in the shotgun, so they add little.)
3. **Two deep safeties** pull you back a notch. Two-high leaves six defenders near the line
   against six blockers, so a run is a fair fight, and offenses like to run against two-high
   and throw against one-high. It doesn't flip the call; it is why this isn't 80%.
4. **The back's offset** doesn't change run-or-pass much. It tells you *which way* a run would
   likely go (from the left, across the quarterback's face, to the right, toward the trips) and
   which side he would protect on a pass.
5. **X's reduced split** tells you about *X*, not about the whole play. Run through its three
   meanings. A crack block fits a run toward him, but the back's offset says a run would go the
   other way, so that one is unlikely. That leaves a route underneath across the middle (a
   [dig](../04-the-passing-game/04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd), which runs ten or so yards
   and cuts flat inside, or a shallow crosser) whose trip the tight split shortens, or a route
   breaking outside, like a corner route toward the sideline, that wants the room he has
   given himself. A slant, the quick cut inside, is the *least* likely: it needs space inside,
   and he has just given it away.

So: "P, 75%, align." Then pick your one thing: X and the cornerback over him, from the snap.
If X cuts inside underneath or breaks for the sideline and the ball goes there, the reduced
split was the tell. If the ball goes elsewhere, check on the replay what X did anyway. That is
how small clues become reliable ones: by checking them, snap after snap, in your log.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **The broadcast is built for the ball.** The main sideline camera keeps the formation tight
  before the snap and chases the ball after it, so the safeties, the outside receivers and most
  of the coverage are off your screen when it matters. Replays exist to give them back: the end
  zone shows the line, the skycam shows the coverage, and the All-22 shows everyone.
- **Use the pause.** Read the scorebug in a fixed order (down and distance, field position,
  score, clock, timeouts) and turn it into a lean before the snap. Down and distance decides the
  lopsided downs; on first-and-10 the formation tells you more.
- **Scan before the snap, then watch one thing**, chosen by your lean: the safeties (or the
  quarterback's first look) when you expect a pass, a guard when you expect a run, the line on
  short yardage, a different group on each replay. The safeties are mostly a replay habit for
  now, because the live shot rarely shows them.
- **Tells are clues, not promises.** Stance, the back's depth and offset, receiver splits and
  safety depth all shift the odds, and the quarterback's alignment shifts them the most. Clues
  that travel together aren't separate evidence. The offense knows its tells too, and
  play-action lives on breaking them.
- **Keep a prediction log**, and score it against the bar: "always pass" gets about 60%, down
  and distance alone about 62%, the whole scorebug about 68%, the scorebug plus the formation
  about 75%.

## Connections

**Builds on:** [The Pre-Snap Phase](01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd) (the motion, shifts and
checks you'll now see during the pause), [What a Play Really Is](01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd)
(the forty seconds that the pause sits at the end of), and
[Downs, Distance, and Field Position](01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd) (your
baseline tally and the situation buckets).

**Sets up:** [Personnel: Who's on the Field Before Anything Else](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd)
adds the first column to your pre-snap read: who came onto the field. The rest of Part 2 adds
formations and a first look at defense, and every later chapter adds a drill to the log.
Further on: [Win Probability and Decision Analysis](../13-analytics-and-data/13-03-win-probability-and-fourth-down.qmd)
and [Tracking Data and the Big Data Bowl](../13-analytics-and-data/13-05-tracking-data-and-big-data-bowl.qmd)
build the numbers glossed here; [Watching Live](../15-capstone/15-01-watching-live.qmd)
completes the tells catalogue and the pre-snap checklist; and
[Film Study: All-22, Charting a Game, and Scoring Yourself](../15-capstone/15-02-film-study-and-charting.qmd)
turns the All-22 into a study routine and scores your season's log.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
- Pat Kirwan, *Take Your Eye Off the Ball* (2010; 2nd ed. 2015): the classic book on exactly
  this chapter's idea, by a former NFL coach and scout, with good sections on what to watch
  before the snap.
- Ron Jaworski with Greg Cosell and David Plaut, *The Games That Changed the Game* (2010):
  seven landmark games, explained by two people who spent careers watching coaches film.
- Chris B. Brown, *The Art of Smart Football* (2015): short essays on why plays are built the
  way they are, which tells you what to look for.
- NFL Next Gen Stats (nextgenstats.nfl.com): the league's own site for the tracking numbers
  broadcasts quote, with weekly leaderboards.
:::

[^wp]: The public nflfastR win-probability model, for example, reports both a situation-only estimate (`wp`) and one that also starts from the pregame point spread (`vegas_wp`): nflverse play-by-play data dictionary, https://nflreadr.nflverse.com/articles/dictionary_pbp.html . How the models are built is in 13-03.

[^ngs]: NFL Football Operations, "NFL Next Gen Stats": RFID tags in each player's shoulder pads and 20–30 receivers in each stadium record location, speed and acceleration 10 times a second: https://operations.nfl.com/gameday/technology/nfl-next-gen-stats/ ; Kevin Seifert, ESPN, "Inside Slant: NFL Next Gen Stats opens new doors" (Dec. 11, 2014), on the 2014 trial in 17 stadiums: https://www.espn.com/blog/nflnation/post/_/id/153569/inside-slant-nfl-next-gen-stats-opens-new-doors

[^ttt]: Course calculation from nflverse participation data (`time_to_throw`, FTN-sourced), 2025 regular season and playoffs: the median time to throw on dropbacks with a recorded time was 2.5 seconds (see also [What a Play Really Is](01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd)).

[^situational]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, 2025 regular season, runs and dropbacks (passes, sacks and scrambles counted as passes): third-and-4 to -6, 91% pass (1,652 snaps); third-and-1, 23% pass (853 snaps).

[^late]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, 2025 regular season: snaps in the last two minutes of the fourth quarter by teams trailing by 1 to 8 points, 87% pass (680 snaps; overtime excluded).

[^qbloc]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play joined to FTN charting (`qb_location`), 2025 regular season, runs and dropbacks: shotgun 78.5% pass (20,104 snaps), under center 31.1% (11,035), pistol 29.3% (1,618).

[^rams]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play joined to FTN charting, 2025 regular season: the Rams' under-center share (59%) and under-center pass rate (40%) were the league's highest; Washington's under-center pass rate (15%) was the lowest. Play-action (`is_play_action`) was used on 82% of under-center dropbacks and 10% of shotgun dropbacks league-wide.

[^idp]: NFL Football Operations, *Official Playing Rules*, penalty summary entry "Ineligible player downfield on pass" (8-3-1): https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/ ; the one-yard limit before a forward pass is thrown: "Ineligible receiver downfield," *Wikipedia* (citing the NFL's *Rules Digest: Forward Pass*): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ineligible_receiver_downfield . The rule itself is taught in [Run-Pass Options](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd).

[^sep]: NFL Next Gen Stats defines average separation as the distance in yards between the receiver and the nearest defender at the time of the catch or incompletion (nflverse Next Gen Stats data dictionary, quoting the NGS definition: https://nflreadr.nflverse.com/articles/dictionary_nextgen_stats.html). Course calculation from nflverse `load_nextgen_stats(stat_type="receiving")`, 2025 regular season, the 120 qualifying receivers: mean 3.0 yards, range 1.9 to 4.6.

[^short]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play joined to FTN charting, 2025 regular season: third-and-1, 23% pass overall (853 snaps) and 16% pass from under center (525 snaps); FTN's `is_qb_sneak` flag (which covers both sneaks and the tush push) marks 31% of those 525 under-center snaps.

[^gun110]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play joined to FTN charting, 2025 regular season, runs and dropbacks: first-and-10 from the shotgun, 72% pass (5,873 snaps).

[^ladder]: Course calculation; the code is in the figure's folded cell. Snaps: 2024 and 2025 regular-season runs and dropbacks with a down recorded (nflverse play-by-play), joined to FTN charting for the quarterback's alignment. Distance buckets 1–3, 4–6 and 7+ yards; score buckets trailing by 9+, trailing by 1–8, tied, leading by 1–8, leading by 9+; "clock" = the last two minutes of either half; "quarter" = fourth quarter or overtime. First-and-10 was 50% pass in 2025 (12,809 snaps); second-and-4 to -6 was 52% (2,623 snaps); second-and-5 to -7 from the shotgun was 76% (1,547 snaps).
